exercises.prompt: What does an esthetic judgment ask about a work?

choices.text: What it does as art
Whether you vote with its author
Whether the price is high
Whether the artist is famous

feedback.note: Esthetic judgment looks at the work as art. Agreement, price, and fame are different questions.

exercises.prompt: Agreeing with a work’s stated ideas is which kind of judgment?

choices.text: A philosophical judgment
Already a full esthetic judgment
A market forecast
A biography of the artist

feedback.note: Sharing a philosophy answers whether you accept the ideas. It does not by itself grade the work as art.

exercises.prompt: Match each question to the kind of judgment it is.

pairs.left: Does this painting hold together as a painting?
Is the novel’s theory of history true?
Did the sculpture make one whole in its medium?

feedback.note: Questions about the work as art stay esthetic. A question about whether a theory is true is philosophical.

exercises.prompt: Complete the unit’s distinction.

parts.text: Judge the work by what it
as art, not by whether you

feedback.note: The two blanks name the split: performance as art on one side, agreement on the other.

exercises.prompt: Build the sentence that states the split.

feedback.note: The judgment and the agreement are neighbors that people mix. They are not the same act.

exercises.prompt: A reader who rejects a novel’s ideas can still do what?

choices.text: Judge whether the novel succeeds as art
Skip judgment, because disagreement ends the question
Treat disagreement as proof the art failed
Copy the ideas in order to be fair

feedback.note: Rejection of the philosophy leaves the esthetic question open. It does not answer it.

exercises.prompt: Which remark mixes the two questions?

choices.text: I disagree, so the book is bad as art.
I disagree, and I still have to judge the art.
The ideas are one issue. The work as art is another.
I can answer each question on its own.

feedback.note: Disagreement is not an esthetic grade. Using it as one collapses the two questions.

exercises.prompt: Match each item to the role it can play.

pairs.left: A clear whole in the medium
A true premise in a separate essay

feedback.note: Only what the work does as art supplies the esthetic evidence. Approval and a side essay do not.

exercises.prompt: Complete the pair of verdicts one person can hold.

parts.text: You can praise the work as

feedback.note: The two verdicts are allowed to differ. Praise of the art is not a signature under the philosophy.

exercises.prompt: Which line is the rule of this unit?

choices.text: Judge the work by what it does as art.
Judge the work by the club the artist joins.
Judge the work by your mood that afternoon.
Judge the work by how old it is.

feedback.note: Club, mood, and age are not the standard. The standard is what the work does as art.

exercises.prompt: As art, what is the work supposed to have done?

choices.text: Presented a selective re-creation, formed as one work
Listed every fact about its subject
Won a vote for a party
Hidden its subject so nothing can be seen

feedback.note: The esthetic question looks for a selective re-creation that stands as a work, not a dump of facts or a campaign.

exercises.prompt: A slogan in the preface, while the work itself is muddled, counts as what?

choices.text: Not a substitute for what the work does
A repair of the work as art
The whole esthetic judgment
The medium of the work

feedback.note: A line beside the work can announce an intention. It cannot do the work’s job for it.

exercises.prompt: Match each item to where it belongs in the judgment.

pairs.left: What is selected and how it is formed

feedback.note: Judgment stays on the re-creation in the work. Talk around it, and the critic’s politics, are not that re-creation.

exercises.prompt: Complete the warning about labels.

feedback.note: A label can name a hope. The esthetic fact is what the work itself does.

exercises.prompt: Build the instruction for this lesson.

feedback.note: The object of judgment is the re-creation on the page, the stage, or the wall, not a caption or a rumor.

exercises.prompt: A painting is judged esthetically by which of these?

choices.text: What the image presents and how it is made
The wall text alone
Who gave the museum the painting
How soft the gallery bench is

feedback.note: The image is the work. A wall text can help a visitor, but it is not the painting.

exercises.prompt: Two works share a message. What follows for esthetic judgment?

choices.text: They can still differ in what they do as art
They must be equal as art
Neither can be judged
The longer one wins

feedback.note: A shared message does not settle the art. Each work is graded by the re-creation it presents.

exercises.prompt: Match each case to what it does as art.

pairs.left: A selective whole that embodies its view
A pile of true facts with no selection
A caption that states the moral for a blank canvas

feedback.note: Truth in a pile, or a moral in a caption, is not yet a selective re-creation.

exercises.prompt: Complete the comparison of two works that share a creed.

feedback.note: The creed can be the same while the works are not. Follow the work.

exercises.prompt: In this unit, “what it does as art” means which of these?

choices.text: What it accomplishes as a selective re-creation
How many ads it sells
How many years the artist spent
How much ink the printer used

feedback.note: Time, ink, and sales are not the accomplishment. The accomplishment is the re-creation the work achieves.

exercises.prompt: A work is highly skilled, and you reject its philosophy. What can you say?

choices.text: It can be strong as art while you reject the view
Skill forces you to accept the view
Rejection forces the skill to count as zero
Skill is not allowed in a work you reject

feedback.note: Skill is about what the work does as art. It does not cast your vote on the philosophy.

exercises.prompt: You accept the philosophy, and the work is clumsy as art. What follows?

choices.text: Agreement does not make the work good art
Agreement repairs the clumsiness
Clumsiness proves the philosophy is false
You must hide the clumsiness

feedback.note: A welcome philosophy cannot stand in for a re-creation the work failed to achieve.

exercises.prompt: Match each split to the fair description.

pairs.left: Skilled projection of a view you reject
pairs.right: Strong as art, disputed as philosophy

pairs.left: Clumsy projection of a view you accept
pairs.right: Welcome as philosophy, weak as art

pairs.left: Treating skill as a vote for the ideas
pairs.right: A mix-up of the two questions

feedback.note: Each direction of the split is possible. Only the third line confuses skill with agreement.

exercises.prompt: Complete the line about what skill is evidence of.

feedback.note: A ballot chooses a view. Skill shows what the work accomplished as art.

exercises.prompt: Build the sentence that keeps skill off the ballot.

feedback.note: You can record the skill and withhold agreement. The skill did not vote.

exercises.prompt: Which report is a fair split?

choices.text: The play is well made, and I still reject its view of man.
The play is well made, so I must accept its view of man.
I reject the view, so the making does not count.
Well made and true-for-me are the same phrase.

feedback.note: The fair report keeps the making and the view in separate columns.

exercises.prompt: Which report is unfair to the art?

choices.text: I share the moral, so the drawing must be good.
I share the moral, and I still look at the drawing.
I share the moral, and the drawing is still weak.
Sharing the moral leaves the drawing to be judged.

feedback.note: A shared moral is not a grade for the drawing. The drawing still has to do its job.

exercises.prompt: Complete the two verbs you may use together.

parts.text: the ideas in the same work.

feedback.note: Admire names the esthetic side. Reject names the philosophical side. Both can stand.

exercises.prompt: Match each act to what it is.

feedback.note: Admiration is not a signature. Calling it agreement mixes the two responses.

exercises.prompt: When does a theme belong inside an esthetic judgment?

choices.text: When the work’s own means carry it
When a footnote states it and the work does not
When a friend explains it after you leave
When a trend says themes are fashionable

feedback.note: The theme counts as part of what the work does only if the means of that work carry it.

exercises.prompt: A lecture stands in for the story, and the story never embodies the point. What is that, as art?

choices.text: A failure to do the job, even if the lecture is true
A success, because truth repairs any story
The best use of a story’s means
Something esthetic judgment must ignore

feedback.note: A true speech is still a speech. If it replaces the art, the work has not done its job as art.

exercises.prompt: Match each case to the judgment it supports.

pairs.left: The theme is shown in the action
pairs.right: The means are doing the work

pairs.left: The theme is announced, and the action never supports it
The medium is ignored so a message can be delivered
pairs.right: The work is not being judged as art

feedback.note: Support inside the work is the test. An announcement, or a message that skips the medium, is not that test.

exercises.prompt: Complete the rule about theme and means.

feedback.note: Through the means is the esthetic path. Around them is a lecture wearing the work’s name.

exercises.prompt: Build the warning about a true sentence.

feedback.note: Truth of a sentence is a philosophical point. It does not become the art by being true.

exercises.prompt: How is a novel’s philosophy relevant to the esthetic question?

choices.text: Only as what the novel must make real in its own story
Only if it is a view you already hold
Only if a character states it at the greatest length
It can never appear in the story at all

feedback.note: The philosophy matters esthetically as the theme the story concretizes, not as a view you prepaid for.

exercises.prompt: In this lesson, what is the failure called when art is used only as a slot for a speech?

choices.text: Letting a lecture replace the means
Selecting and forming a re-creation
Keeping esthetic and philosophical questions apart
Showing skill you do not agree with

feedback.note: The failure is substitution: the speech does the talking, and the means of the art do not.

exercises.prompt: Match each case to its role.

pairs.left: An image that embodies the meaning
A note that tells you what to feel while the image is mud
Your prior agreement with the meaning
pairs.right: Not a means of the work

feedback.note: Embodiment is the painting’s job. A scolding note, and your prior agreement, are not means of that painting.

exercises.prompt: Complete the test.

parts.text: the theme, the work has not

feedback.note: Carry and done name the test: the means either achieve the theme as art, or they do not.

exercises.prompt: Which question closes this lesson?

choices.text: Do this work’s means actually carry its theme?
Does the author belong to my club?
Is the speech the longest chapter?
Is the theme true, and can I stop there?

feedback.note: Stop on the means. Club membership, length, and bare truth do not answer whether the work carried its theme.

exercises.prompt: You dislike the philosophy. What happens to the esthetic standard?

choices.text: It stays the same
It is dropped
It reverses so failure counts as success
It becomes your mood

feedback.note: Dislike changes your philosophical answer. It does not rewrite the esthetic standard.

exercises.prompt: You love the philosophy. What happens to the esthetic standard?

choices.text: It stays the same
It softens so any effort counts as success
It no longer applies
It becomes loyalty to the author

feedback.note: Love of the ideas is not a softer ruler. The work is still judged by what it does as art.

exercises.prompt: Match each situation to the right move.

pairs.left: A work you love that is poorly made
pairs.right: Say so under the esthetic standard

pairs.left: A work you oppose that is strongly made
pairs.right: Say so under the same standard

pairs.left: A work you have not taken in

feedback.note: The standard applies in both directions, and only to a work you have actually taken in.

exercises.prompt: Complete the rule of application.

parts.text: for works you welcome and works you

feedback.note: Welcome and oppose are philosophical postures. They share one esthetic standard.

exercises.prompt: Build the instruction to keep the ruler steady.

feedback.note: Either way means when you agree and when you do not. Softer and louder are not the standard.

exercises.prompt: Which report keeps the questions apart?

choices.text: As art it fails to integrate, though I agree with the author.
As art it fails because I disagree.
As art it succeeds because I agree.
I never say what it does as art.

feedback.note: The first report gives the art its own grade and the philosophy a separate one.

exercises.prompt: Which report collapses the two questions?

choices.text: It fails as art because I disagree.
It is strongly made, and I disagree.
It is weakly made, and I agree.
I ask what it does as art before I grade it.

feedback.note: Because I disagree is a philosophical reason dressed up as an esthetic grade.

exercises.prompt: Match each question to its job.

pairs.left: What does it do as art?

feedback.note: Name the question first. Then the grade lands on art or on agreement, not on a blur of both.

exercises.prompt: Build the closing instruction.

feedback.note: Apart means each judgment gets its own answer: what the work does as art, and whether you agree.

exercises.prompt: What does esthetics study, in the branch where this unit sits?

choices.text: Art
The proper use of force
Laboratory measurement
Table manners

feedback.note: Esthetics is the study of art. Romanticism is placed inside that study, not in politics or in a lab.

exercises.prompt: In this unit, what names a school of art?

choices.text: Its basic view of man
The century on the copyright page
How bright the colors are
The artist's childhood

feedback.note: A school is a fundamental view of man as art presents him. Date, palette, and biography do not name the school.

exercises.prompt: Match each name to the job this unit gives it.

pairs.right: A basic view of man in art

feedback.note: Keep the three levels apart: the branch, the kind of classification, and the school this unit teaches.

exercises.prompt: Complete the placement.

feedback.note: It sits inside esthetics as a school. It is not an extra branch beside metaphysics, epistemology, ethics, and politics, and it is not a mood.

exercises.prompt: Build the sentence that places the school.

feedback.note: The school is an esthetic classification. Politics is a different branch.

exercises.prompt: Which name does this unit use for the school committed to volition?

choices.text: Romanticism
Naturalism
Etiquette
Skepticism

feedback.note: Romanticism is the name of that commitment. Naturalism is the contrast you will meet later, not this name.

exercises.prompt: What is the second job of this unit, after naming the commitment?

choices.text: To place the school in her esthetics
To rank living painters by fame
To set ticket prices
To draft a statute

feedback.note: The unit teaches the commitment to volition and where that school sits in her esthetics. Fame, price, and statutes are outside it.

exercises.prompt: Complete the commitment named in the unit summary.

feedback.note: Volition is the commitment. Fashion, nostalgia, and luck are not what the school is named for.

exercises.prompt: Build the sentence about what a school states.

feedback.note: The classification is a view of man. Weather is scenery, not the school.

exercises.prompt: What premise defines Romanticism?

choices.text: Man possesses volition
Glands write a man's course
Class origin fixes every end
The stars decree each act

feedback.note: The school stands on volition: man can choose. Forces that erase choice are the opposite premise.

exercises.prompt: Under that premise, what sets a character's course?

choices.text: Choice
Weather alone
The street name alone
Blood type alone

feedback.note: Setting can matter, but the Romantic premise is that the person chooses a course rather than only undergoing one.

exercises.prompt: Match each idea to what the premise says about it.

pairs.right: Possible because a choice can be wrong

feedback.note: If choice is real, a person can pick a value, pursue it, and also miss. That is the premise at work.

exercises.prompt: Complete the defining claim.

feedback.note: The faculty named here is volition. The school does not claim that man knows everything, cannot be hurt, or holds a title.

exercises.prompt: Build the sentence that states the premise.

feedback.note: Can choose is the premise. Cannot would cancel the school.

exercises.prompt: In this unit, volition means which power?

choices.text: The power to choose
A talent for feeling strongly
Physical strength
Social status

feedback.note: Volition is the faculty of choice. Intensity of feeling, muscle, and status are different facts.

exercises.prompt: A story insists the hero could not have done otherwise. What has happened to the Romantic premise?

choices.text: The premise has been dropped
The premise has been proved
The premise has been doubled
The premise has just been named

feedback.note: If no alternative was open, choice was not real in that story. That is a dropped premise, not a proof of it.

exercises.prompt: Name what the school will not drop.

feedback.note: Costume, dialect, and scenery can change. The premise that stays is choice.

exercises.prompt: Match each case to the premise it shows.

feedback.note: The test is whether choice is real. Values pursued by decision are what that reality looks like in the work.

exercises.prompt: Build the sentence about characters.

feedback.note: Action by choice is the premise in story form. Reflex and drift are not substitutes for it.

exercises.prompt: Which view is the contrast to Romanticism in this unit?

choices.text: Man is a product of forces he does not choose
Man possesses volition
Maps should be drawn to scale
Every line must rhyme

feedback.note: The opposing view denies choice and treats man as determined by forces. Scale and rhyme are not the contrast.

exercises.prompt: In this contrast, what does Naturalism do with volition?

choices.text: It denies volition
It is the name of the volitional school
It proves that anyone can choose
It is only a rule about paintbrushes

feedback.note: Naturalism, as the contrast here, is the school that denies volition. Romanticism is the school that holds it.

exercises.prompt: Match each school to its stand on choice.

feedback.note: The split is volition versus the denial of volition. That is the whole contrast between the two schools.

exercises.prompt: Complete the contrast.

feedback.note: Denies is the relation. Naturalism is not a hymn to volition and not a brush technique.

exercises.prompt: Build the sentence about a determined man.

feedback.note: Determination, in this contrast, means the course is not chosen. That is why it is not Romanticism.

exercises.prompt: Heredity and the street alone decide the ending. Which premise is the story carrying?

choices.text: Not the Romantic premise
The Romantic premise in full
Both schools at once, with no difference
No view of man at all, by definition

feedback.note: If only unchosen forces decide the end, the story is not carrying the premise that man chooses.

exercises.prompt: Both schools can use realistic detail. What actually splits them?

choices.text: Whether man is shown as able to choose
Whether the furniture looks dusty
Whether the book is long
Whether the ink is black

feedback.note: Realistic detail can appear on either side. The school is fixed by the view of choice, not by how solid the furniture looks.

exercises.prompt: Complete the line about the split.

parts.text: , not about how real the furniture looks.

feedback.note: Volition is the issue. Upholstery, page count, and ink do not classify the school.

exercises.prompt: Build the sentence about what does not decide the school.

feedback.note: Detail is not the classifier. Volition is, which is why it is the distractor you leave out of this sentence.

exercises.prompt: Does feeling strongly, by itself, make a work Romantic?

choices.text: No
Yes, intensity is the definition
Only if the feeling is sadness
Only if the audience cries

feedback.note: Intensity is not the definition. The school is a commitment to volition, not a measure of how hard someone feels.

exercises.prompt: Is escape from the facts what Romanticism is committed to?

choices.text: No. The commitment is volition, not a cancellation of facts
Yes. The school exists to leave reality
Yes, if the setting is a dream
Yes, if the costumes are old

feedback.note: The school re-creates a world in which people choose. It does not mean flight from facts, dreams, or period costume.

exercises.prompt: Match each popular stand-in to what this unit says about it.

feedback.note: Feeling and mysticism are common mix-ups. Volition is what the school actually commits to.

exercises.prompt: Complete the correction.

feedback.note: Mood, fog, and costume can decorate any school. They do not replace the commitment to volition.

exercises.prompt: Build the sentence that rejects the mix-up.

feedback.note: Emotion does not define it. The distractor would reverse the point.

exercises.prompt: A gloomy mystical tale shows no chosen action. Is it Romantic just because it is intense?

choices.text: No
Yes, gloom is enough
Yes, if a castle appears
Yes, if the music swells

feedback.note: Intensity, gloom, castles, and swelling music do not supply the premise. Without chosen action, it is not this school.

exercises.prompt: A bright adventure shows nothing chosen. Does the cheerful tone make it Romantic?

choices.text: No. Tone is not the test
Yes. Brightness is the test
Yes, if the pace is fast
Yes, if someone is called a hero

feedback.note: Cheer and gloom are both tones. The test remains whether the work treats man as able to choose.

exercises.prompt: Build the sentence that names the test.

feedback.note: Choice is the test. Intensity and costume are the mix-ups this lesson sets aside.

exercises.prompt: Because man can choose, what can a work show besides events that are only endured?

choices.text: Values selected and pursued
Nothing but the weather report
Nothing but a list of objects
Nothing a person could aim at

feedback.note: Volition makes selected values visible. A list or a weather report does not use that premise.

exercises.prompt: Why does purposeful action belong to this school?

choices.text: Purpose presupposes a chooser
Purpose is only a rhyme scheme
Purpose means the work is short
Purpose means a crowd agrees

feedback.note: A purpose is an end someone chooses to pursue. Without a chooser, the action is not purposeful in this sense.

exercises.prompt: Match each term to its role in this unit.

pairs.right: Action aimed at a chosen end
The branch where the school is placed

feedback.note: Volition is the premise, purpose is what that premise lets action be, and esthetics is where the school is classified.

exercises.prompt: Complete why the school belongs in her esthetics.

parts.text: It belongs there because she takes man to be a being of

feedback.note: Her view of man is volitional consciousness. Romanticism is the esthetic school that projects that fact, not an automatic, tribal, or merely decorative premise.

exercises.prompt: Build the sentence that links purpose to choice.

feedback.note: A chooser is required. A crowd count or a rhyme does not supply a purpose.

exercises.prompt: Where does Romanticism sit, and what does it not replace?

choices.text: Inside esthetics, as the school that projects volition
It replaces ethics
It replaces politics
It replaces arithmetic

feedback.note: The place is inside esthetics. The school does not stand in for ethics, politics, or arithmetic.

exercises.prompt: What does this unit fix about a work, and what does it leave for later?

choices.text: It fixes the school by the volition premise, and leaves other standards of judgment for later
It fixes the market price
It fixes which prize the work must win
It fixes a legal ban

feedback.note: This unit identifies the school. Judging a work by the full standards of art is a further question, not this lesson.

exercises.prompt: Match each branch to what it covers, so the place of this school stays clear.

feedback.note: Romanticism is not a code of living and not a theory of force. It is a school inside the study of art.

exercises.prompt: Complete what the school projects.

parts.text: Romanticism projects man as able to

feedback.note: The projection is a being who can choose. Vanishing, mere obedience, and floating are not that projection.

exercises.prompt: Build the sentence that states the projection.

feedback.note: That projection is the place of Romanticism in her esthetics: art that presents man as a being who chooses.

exercises.prompt: On this account, what is art?

choices.text: A selective re-creation of reality according to metaphysical value-judgments
An unedited copy of whatever happens to be in front of the artist
A private mood with no tie to reality
Any object someone calls useful

feedback.note: The unit’s definition has three parts: selection, a re-creation of reality, and metaphysical value-judgments.

exercises.prompt: Which word names the thing art re-creates?

choices.text: Reality
A wish that replaces facts
A public vote
A fashion label by itself

feedback.note: Art re-creates reality. It does not start from nothing and it does not treat wishes as a substitute for what is.

exercises.prompt: Match each part of the definition to what it names.

pairs.right: The artist chooses what to include
The work presents reality again, shaped by that choice
The standard that guides the choice

feedback.note: Drop any one of the three parts and the definition is no longer the one this unit teaches.

exercises.prompt: Complete the definition.

feedback.note: Selective names the choice. Reality names what is re-created.

exercises.prompt: Build the definition in order.

feedback.note: The order is the claim: art, then selective re-creation, then of reality, then the standard of selection.

exercises.prompt: What does the definition rule out as a full account of art?

choices.text: An unselective dump of everything the artist notices
A chosen presentation of reality
A work shaped by a view of existence
Selection guided by what the artist takes as fundamental

feedback.note: If nothing is selected, the work is not the kind of re-creation the definition names.

exercises.prompt: Whose judgments set the selection, on this definition?

choices.text: The artist’s metaphysical value-judgments
Whatever a crowd happens to like that day
No one’s; selection needs no standard
Only the price of the materials

feedback.note: The according-to clause names the artist’s metaphysical value-judgments as the standard of what is chosen.

exercises.prompt: A metaphysical value-judgment, in this definition, is a judgment about what?

choices.text: What is fundamental about man and existence
Only the market price of the work
Only spelling and grammar
Only the weather on the day it was made

feedback.note: Metaphysical here means a judgment about the nature of existence, not a tip about technique or sales.

exercises.prompt: Match each mistaken slogan to the part of the definition it drops.

pairs.left: Art is whatever spills out, unchosen
Art invents a world with no reality in it
Art chooses, but by no view of existence

feedback.note: Each slogan keeps some words of the definition and throws away one essential part.

exercises.prompt: Name the standard that guides the selection.

parts.text: The selection follows the artist’s metaphysical

feedback.note: Value-judgments of a metaphysical kind are the according-to clause of the definition.

exercises.prompt: What does selective mean in this definition?

choices.text: The artist chooses which aspects to include, omit, and stress
The artist must include every fact equally
The artist must avoid anything real
The work is finished by chance

feedback.note: Selection is a choice among aspects of reality, not a refusal of reality and not a dump of all of it.

exercises.prompt: Leaving something out of a work is compatible with the definition when the omission is what?

choices.text: Part of a deliberate selection
Proof that reality was never the subject
Always a failure to copy the whole world
Forbidden by the word re-creation

feedback.note: Re-creation is selective, so omission is how the artist isolates what the work is about.

exercises.prompt: Match each act of selection to what it does.

pairs.right: Puts an aspect into the work
Leaves an aspect out on purpose
Makes one included aspect stand out

feedback.note: Include, omit, and stress are three ways the same selection is carried out.

exercises.prompt: Fill in what the artist does not do.

parts.text: A selective re-creation is not an

feedback.note: If every detail stayed in at equal weight, nothing would have been selected.

exercises.prompt: Put the idea of selection in order.

feedback.note: Choice among real aspects is selection. Total inclusion and total rejection of reality are not.

exercises.prompt: Two painters look at the same city. One stresses human achievement and omits decay. The other does the reverse. What does the definition say they differ in?

choices.text: What each selects as worth presenting
Whether a city can exist
Whether either of them has eyes
Nothing; the same subject forces the same work

feedback.note: The same reality can be re-created under different selections. That is what selective allows.

exercises.prompt: Stressing one feature means what?

choices.text: Giving that feature more weight than other included features
Erasing the feature so it cannot be seen
Replacing reality with a feature that could not exist
Listing every feature at the same size

feedback.note: Stress is still selection inside what was included. It is emphasis, not a denial that the feature is real.

exercises.prompt: Which job is not what selective means?

choices.text: Taking a census of every fact with no emphasis
Omitting what does not serve the work
Keeping what the artist judges essential
Ranking some aspects above others

feedback.note: A census tries not to select. Art, on this definition, must select.

exercises.prompt: Match the practice to selective or not selective.

pairs.left: Isolating one human choice as the center of a story
Keeping every street noise because it occurred
Cutting a scene that does not bear on the theme

feedback.note: Selection is purposeful inclusion and omission. Recording an event only because it happened is not that.

exercises.prompt: Name the three moves of selection.

feedback.note: Include, omit, and stress are the concrete meaning of selective in this unit.

feedback.note: The three pieces do different work. Dropping any one of them shortens the claim.

exercises.prompt: Match each case to the response.

pairs.left: Art is only for spare cash
A mind of concepts needs art

feedback.note: Spare cash and decorate-later are the two refusals. The positive claim is the conceptual mind’s need.

exercises.prompt: Complete the full claim.

parts.text: Art is a need of a conceptual consciousness, not a

feedback.note: Luxury is the word the full sentence refuses. The other bank words belong on the positive side of the claim.

exercises.prompt: Fill both sides.

parts.text: mind, and it is not added after thought is

feedback.note: Conceptual names the mind. Finished names the timing that does not apply.

exercises.prompt: Build the full claim’s opening.

feedback.note: The opening states the positive half. Luxury and afterward are the halves this sentence is not using.

exercises.prompt: Build the refusal that completes the claim.

feedback.note: The refusal is not a luxury after thought is finished. That closing belongs with the positive half.

exercises.prompt: What is a theme?

choices.text: The work's abstract meaning
The list of events in order
How skilled the artist is
What the work sold for

feedback.note: A theme is the work's abstract meaning, not a record of events, a rating of skill, or a market fact.

exercises.prompt: Match each phrase to what it names in a work.

feedback.note: The theme is the meaning. The concretes are what the artist put in. They are what carry the meaning.

exercises.prompt: Complete the name of a theme.

feedback.note: Abstract means the meaning is a general idea, not one isolated fact sitting beside the work.

exercises.prompt: Build the unit's claim in order.

feedback.note: Keep both parts: the theme is abstract meaning, and that meaning is carried by the concretes.

exercises.prompt: Which of these could be a theme?

choices.text: A person can remake a life by choice
The story has three named people
The book is two hundred pages
The cover is blue

feedback.note: A theme is a meaning you can state in general terms. A head count, a length, or a color is not a meaning.

exercises.prompt: Match each candidate to theme or not a theme.

pairs.left: Justice can fail when people look away

feedback.note: Only the first item states an abstract meaning. Length and medium are facts about the object, not its theme.

exercises.prompt: Fill the two words that name what a theme is.

feedback.note: Those two words are the core. Everything else in the unit says how that meaning gets into the work.

exercises.prompt: A theme belongs to which of these?

choices.text: The work, as its abstract meaning
Only the loudest fan's mood
The shelf the book sits on
The price of a ticket

feedback.note: The theme is the work's meaning. A viewer's mood or a price tag is not a substitute for it.

exercises.prompt: A plot summary mainly reports what?

choices.text: What happens, in the concretes
The abstract meaning those events carry
Which esthetic school the artist joined
Whether you agree with the artist

feedback.note: A summary stays with the events. A theme states the abstract meaning those events are there to carry.

exercises.prompt: Match each sentence to plot or theme.

pairs.left: She leaves the town after the trial
Integrity can cost a place in the group
He finds the letter in the desk

feedback.note: Leaving, a trial, and a letter are concretes. Integrity and its cost are the kind of meaning a theme states.

exercises.prompt: Complete the contrast.

parts.text: A plot recounts events. A theme states

feedback.note: Do not stop at what happened. Ask what abstract meaning those happenings carry.

exercises.prompt: Order the contrast.

feedback.note: Plot answers what happens. Theme answers what that sequence means in abstract terms.

exercises.prompt: Someone says the theme is that the hero crosses a river. What went wrong?

choices.text: That names an event, not an abstract meaning
Nothing. An event is already a theme
The sentence is too short to be a plot
A theme must include the hero's name

feedback.note: Crossing a river is a concrete event. The theme would be the abstract meaning that crossing is used to carry.

exercises.prompt: Match the question to the answer it seeks.

feedback.note: Who appears and what they do are concretes. The theme is the meaning those choices carry.

exercises.prompt: Two works share the same chase scene. Must they share a theme?

choices.text: No. The same kind of event can carry different meanings
Yes. Matching events fix the theme
Only if both works are short
No event can carry any meaning

feedback.note: A chase is a concrete. What it means depends on the meaning the whole choice of concretes carries.

exercises.prompt: Finish the warning.

parts.text: Retelling the events is not yet stating the

feedback.note: A retelling stays at the concretes. The theme is the abstract meaning those concretes carry.

exercises.prompt: Which line is closer to a theme than to a plot note?

choices.text: Courage is acting when the outcome is not guaranteed
She opens the door at midnight
It rains in chapter two
He wears a gray hat

feedback.note: The first line states an abstract meaning. The others report details a plot summary might include.

exercises.prompt: In this unit, what carries the theme?

choices.text: The concretes the artist chose
A preface written by someone else
A review printed later
The shipping crate

feedback.note: The theme is carried by the concretes the artist chose, not by packaging or by a later comment.

exercises.prompt: Match each concrete to the art it could belong to.

pairs.left: A named action in a story
A figure placed in a painting
A musical phrase set against silence

feedback.note: Concretes differ by art. In each case they are the particulars the artist chose to carry the meaning.

exercises.prompt: Complete the carrier.

parts.text: The theme is carried by the

feedback.note: Chosen concretes are the carrier. Outside talk about the work is not a substitute carrier.

exercises.prompt: Build the relation.

feedback.note: Choice of concretes and the meaning they carry belong together. The theme is not parked outside the work.

exercises.prompt: Why say the artist chose the concretes?

choices.text: The particulars in the work are there by the artist's selection
Every fact in the world is automatically in the work
Concretes appear with no one deciding
The audience inserts the concretes later

feedback.note: A work does not contain everything. The concretes that carry the theme are the ones the artist chose.

exercises.prompt: Match each item to inside the work or outside it.

feedback.note: Only what the artist put into the work is a concrete that can carry its theme. Talk about the work is not the work.

exercises.prompt: An artist drops a scene that pointed another way. What changed?

choices.text: The set of concretes that carry the meaning
Nothing, because theme ignores concretes
The legal status of the audience
The calendar year of the reader's birth

feedback.note: Leaving a scene out changes which concretes are there to carry the theme. The carrier is the set the artist kept.

exercises.prompt: Fill both blanks.

feedback.note: Meaning is the theme. Concretes are the carrier. Both words are required.

exercises.prompt: Which list is a list of concretes rather than a theme?

choices.text: A bridge, a storm, and a refusal to turn back
Resolve holds when conditions turn against you
Both lines are themes
Neither line has anything to do with a work

feedback.note: Bridge, storm, and refusal are particulars. The sentence about resolve is the kind of abstract meaning they might carry.

exercises.prompt: A poster beside a painting says what the painting means, but the image shows none of it. Where is the theme of the painting?

choices.text: Only in what the image's concretes actually carry
In the poster, which replaces the image
The poster becomes part of the painting automatically
Paintings cannot have a theme

feedback.note: A slogan next to the work is not the carrier. The theme has to be carried by the concretes the artist chose.

exercises.prompt: Match each case to carried or merely pasted.

pairs.left: The actions show the meaning the author names
A last sentence announces a meaning the story never shows
A caption states a moral the picture does not present

feedback.note: Carried means the concretes present the meaning. Pasted means the meaning is only announced from outside those concretes.

exercises.prompt: Complete the standard.

feedback.note: Carried is the verb in this unit. A meaning that the concretes do not carry is not the work's theme.

exercises.prompt: Order the check.

feedback.note: Start from the chosen concretes. The theme is the abstract meaning they carry, not a line attached later.

exercises.prompt: The artist can state the theme in an essay. Does that statement replace the work?

choices.text: No. In the work, the concretes still have to carry it
Yes. An essay is the theme of every work by that artist
Only if the essay is shorter than the work
No artist may say what a work means

feedback.note: An outside statement can name a meaning. Inside the work, that meaning still has to be carried by the concretes.

exercises.prompt: A story's events all show betrayal, and the last line says the theme is loyalty. Which meaning did the concretes carry?

choices.text: Betrayal, the meaning the events present
Loyalty, because the last line says so
Both equally, with no role for the events
Neither, because stories have no theme

feedback.note: When the announcement and the concretes conflict, the theme of the work is the meaning the concretes carry.

exercises.prompt: Match the mistake to what it confuses.

pairs.left: Treating a plot note as the theme
Treating a slogan as the theme
Treating a review as the theme
pairs.right: Outside talk instead of the work

feedback.note: The theme is abstract meaning, and it is carried by the work's own concretes. Events, slogans, and reviews each miss one of those.

exercises.prompt: Finish the contrast.

parts.text: A pasted slogan is not a substitute for meaning

feedback.note: Pasting a moral beside the work does not make that moral the theme. The concretes have to carry it.

exercises.prompt: Which sentence states this unit's full claim?

choices.text: A theme is the work's abstract meaning, carried by the concretes the artist chose
A theme is whatever a reviewer feels that day
A theme is the order of chapters
A theme is a sense of life, and nothing further

feedback.note: Keep both halves. Abstract meaning names the theme. The chosen concretes are what carry it.

exercises.prompt: Match each half of the claim to its job.

feedback.note: The two halves answer different questions: what the meaning is, and what in the work carries it.

exercises.prompt: Assemble the full claim.

feedback.note: Drop the distractors. The claim is meaning plus the concretes that carry it, not a review and not the plot.

exercises.prompt: Complete both halves.

parts.text: , carried by the concretes the artist

feedback.note: Meaning names the theme. Chose names the artist's selection of the concretes that carry it.

exercises.prompt: A reader reports only the events and never the meaning. What is missing?

choices.text: The theme, the abstract meaning those events carry
The events, which were never mentioned
The sale price
The name of an esthetic school

feedback.note: Events are the concretes. Without the abstract meaning they carry, the theme has not been stated.

exercises.prompt: A reader states a grand meaning and never looks at what the artist put in the work. What is missing?

choices.text: The concretes that would have to carry that meaning
Nothing, because a meaning needs no carrier
The typeface of the title
The city where the reader lives

feedback.note: An abstract meaning becomes the work's theme only as what the chosen concretes carry.

exercises.prompt: Match the reader's move to the verdict.

pairs.left: States a meaning the concretes carry
Stops at a list of events
pairs.right: Has the plot, not the theme

pairs.left: Quotes a slogan the work does not present
pairs.right: Has a paste-on, not the theme

feedback.note: Only the first move keeps abstract meaning and the chosen concretes together.

exercises.prompt: One last completion.

parts.text: The theme is not the plot and not a slogan. It is

feedback.note: That is the whole unit: abstract meaning, carried by the concretes the artist chose.

exercises.prompt: Two readers name the same abstract meaning. One can point to the concretes that carry it. The other cannot. Who has shown the theme of this work?

choices.text: The reader who ties the meaning to the chosen concretes
The reader who only announces the meaning
Neither, because a theme cannot be shown
Both equally, because concretes do not matter

feedback.note: Showing the theme means showing the abstract meaning as what these concretes carry, not merely saying a general idea.

exercises.prompt: Put the check in the order this unit uses.

tokens.text: Point to the concretes that carry it

feedback.note: First the meaning, then the concretes that carry it. A poster or a refusal to look at the work does not complete the claim.
